around.headline: Woman fights off molester on Bengaluru bus; police launch manhunt after video goes viral
around.summary: A video of a woman on a BMTC bus fighting off a man who harassed her has gone viral, and police have launched a manhunt to identify and arrest him. If you witness or experience harassment on a bus, recording it and flagging it to the conductor or police immediately can help build a case exactly like this one.
around.source: The Times of India / The Indian Express

around.headline: Bengaluru traffic head constable suspended over ₹5,000 bribe from lorry driver
around.summary: A head constable has been suspended after being caught taking a ₹5,000 bribe from a lorry driver in a traffic violation case, days after two other personnel were filmed accepting cash from motorists. Always ask for an official challan instead of paying cash on the spot, and report bribe demands via the Bengaluru Traffic Police app or the Karnataka Lokayukta.
around.source: Deccan Herald / The Times of India

around.headline: Bengaluru Metro reportedly breaching official fare cap; commuters seek correction
around.summary: Commuters have flagged that fares on some Namma Metro routes exceed the government-mandated cap and are pushing for a correction. If your fare looks off, note the exact route and amount and raise it through BMRCL's official app or helpline rather than arguing at the gate.

around.headline: BMTC rolls out two new AC buses on Electronics City route from Monday
around.summary: BMTC is adding two new air-conditioned buses connecting the city to Electronics City starting Monday — a useful AC alternative if you commute to the tech corridor.

around.headline: 125 volunteers give Silk Board junction a makeover
around.summary: A group of 125 volunteers carried out a cleanup and makeover of the perennially congested Silk Board junction. A small but visible sign of citizen-led civic upkeep at one of the city's most notorious traffic pinch points.

around.headline: Bengaluru's air quality fails to clear as PM10 levels stay elevated
around.summary: Particulate matter (PM10) readings across the city remain high enough to keep pollution concerns going. If you have respiratory sensitivities, it's worth checking today's AQI before spending extended time outdoors, especially near traffic corridors.

around.headline: Nilekani to lead national task force on exam reforms as new Exam Bill proposes tougher paper-leak penalties
around.summary: PM Modi has named Nandan Nilekani to head a task force on exam reforms, alongside a new Exam Bill promising stricter punishments and faster trials for paper-leak cases. It lands the same week Bengaluru's own 20-year-old PG entrance paper-leak case is still without a trial — a reminder of how long these cases can drag on locally even as national rules tighten.
around.source: The Hindu / News18 / The Times of India

street_smart.title: The metro gate reader shows a fare higher than what's posted for your route. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: Real report today: commuters flagged that Bengaluru Metro is charging fares above the government-mandated cap and are seeking a correction (The New Indian Express).
street_smart.situation: You tap in at the gate and the fare deducted is noticeably more than what's listed for your route on the station's fare chart. There's a queue building behind you.

choices.text: Note the date, time, station, and the exact fare charged, then raise it through BMRCL's official app, helpline, or written complaint asking for the fare-cap correction.
choices.feedback: Correct. Gate staff usually can't authorise refunds on the spot, so a documented complaint through the official channel is what actually gets a fare corrected — and it adds to the pressure that's already built today's news story.

choices.text: Ignore it — it's only a few rupees difference.
choices.feedback: Small overcharges add up across thousands of daily riders, and if nobody flags it, there's no pressure on the operator to fix it. It's not dangerous, but it does let a systemic problem slide.

choices.text: Argue loudly with the gate staff and refuse to let others through until you're refunded.
choices.feedback: Station staff at the gate typically don't have the authority to process fare-cap refunds — you'll just cause a scene and hold up other commuters without actually fixing the charge.

choices.text: A stranger near the gate offers to 'sort your refund' right now for a small fee if you scan his QR code.
choices.feedback: This is the trap. No legitimate refund or fare-correction process ever needs you to pay a stranger a fee first, or scan an unknown QR code — that's a payment-redirect scam preying on commuters who are already annoyed and want a quick fix. Official corrections come from BMRCL, not someone loitering at the gate.

takeaways: Fare or ticketing disputes on Metro/BMTC should go through the operator's official app, helpline, or written complaint — not an argument with gate staff who can't authorise refunds.
No legitimate refund or correction process ever asks you to pay a fee or scan a QR code first — that's always a scam pattern.
Keep your ticket or QR code and note the exact fare charged versus the posted cap; documentation is what gets a correction actually actioned.

quiz.q: In monetary policy, what does the 'repo rate' refer to?
options: The interest rate at which the RBI lends short-term funds to commercial banks
The interest rate banks pay depositors
The exchange rate between the rupee and the dollar
The tax rate on repossessed property
quiz.why: Its counterpart, the 'reverse repo rate,' is the rate at which the RBI borrows money back from banks — together they're key levers for controlling inflation and liquidity.
